The data clearly show higher PFOS removal than PFOA under the reported conditions and attribute this to higher affinity of PFOS sulfonate groups for iron/aluminum and to hydrophobic/electrostatic interactions. The mechanistic explanations are phrased as attributions and likelihoods, not as directly demonstrated mechanisms. An additional study with iron oxide solids and GAC shows condition-specific changes in selectivity (greater PFOA sorption increase with negligible change in PFOS), reinforcing that iron effects are system-dependent. Thus the question is answerable with the supplied evidence, while avoiding generalization beyond the studied systems.

In the iron-containing green sorption media studied by Ordonez et al. (IFGEM-7 and AGEM-2, which contain sand, clay, and recycled iron and/or aluminum), PFOS consistently shows higher removal than PFOA under the reported conditions. The authors state that “PFOS can be removed more efﬁciently than PFOA from water by green sorption media,” and batch tests show PFOS removal efficiencies ranging from 27–46% and 23–42%, while PFOA removal efficiencies are much lower, 6–16% and 5–18% for IFGEM-7 and AGEM-2, respectively. In column experiments, the initial (within 1 h) removal by IFGEM-7 is reported as greater than 99% for PFOS and 28% for PFOA. The conclusion summarizes that, as evidenced by these batch and column studies, there is “higher removal of PFOS compared to PFOA,” indicating compound-selective behavior favoring PFOS in these media.

The primary affinity explanation offered for this selectivity is that PFOS’s sulfonate headgroup interacts more strongly with iron- or aluminum-bearing phases than PFOA’s carboxylate headgroup. Specifically, the authors state that the higher PFOS removal “can be attributed to the higher afﬁnity of sulfonate groups of PFOS toward iron or aluminum when compared to that of the carboxylate groups of PFOA,” and reiterate that “the higher percentage removal of PFOS compared to that of PFOA can be attributed to higher afﬁnity of sulfonate groups of PFOS toward iron or aluminum when compared to that of the carboxylate groups of PFOA.” A similar statement appears in the results section, noting that “the higher removal of PFOS can be attributed to higher afﬁnity of sulfonate groups of PFOS toward irons or alumina when compared to the that of the carboxylate groups of PFOA.” These passages frame the affinity explanation as an attribution based on observed removal patterns and prior literature, rather than as a mechanism that is directly demonstrated (for example, no independent binding measurements are reported in the provided text).

The study also proposes additional interaction mechanisms that may contribute to PFOS and PFOA sorption in these green media. With sand as the main ingredient, the authors state that PFOS and PFOA removal “may be primarily governed by hydrophobic interactions,” and that “electrostatic interactions from clay and iron coupled with the hydrophilic ﬁlms surrounding the iron particles appear to further promote adsorption.” Under dynamic adsorption, they further note that the “high removals of PFOS and PFOA could be attributed to a combination of electrostatic and hydrophobic interactions of the compounds with sand and clay particles” and that removals were “likely facilitated by their electrostatic interactions with clay and iron coupled with the adsorption promoted by the hydrophilic ﬁlms surrounding the iron particles.” They also suggest that the higher PFOS removal “could be attributed to the synergistic interactions of PFOS with sand, clay, and ZVI.” The modal language (“may,” “could be attributed,” “likely facilitated”) indicates that these are proposed mechanisms to rationalize the performance, not mechanisms conclusively demonstrated by separate mechanistic assays.

A separate GAC study with iron oxide solids illustrates that iron-containing phases can influence PFOS and PFOA differently in other systems. For granular activated carbons F400 and CBC, the presence of iron oxide solids increased the extent of PFOA sorption by 4.5 mg/g (46%) and 3.8 mg/g (45%), respectively, while PFOS exhibited negligible change (<1 mg/L [10%]) in the presence of iron oxide. The authors add that, although PFAS can sorb onto iron oxide–rich materials, “the influence of iron oxide is expected to be minor compared to the GAC sorption capacity.” This shows that iron oxide can differentially affect PFOA versus PFOS sorption in a GAC system, but that its impact is described as minor relative to the underlying carbon sorption.

Taken together, the supplied evidence supports that, for the specific iron-containing green sorption media tested, PFOS is removed more effectively than PFOA, and this behavior is attributed to higher affinity of PFOS sulfonate groups toward iron or aluminum plus hydrophobic and electrostatic interactions with the media components. These explanations are presented as attributions and likely mechanisms grounded in observed performance and prior literature, rather than as mechanisms directly proven by independent mechanistic measurements. In a different system (GAC with iron oxide solids), iron oxide has a larger relative effect on PFOA than PFOS, underscoring that PFOS-versus-PFOA selectivity in iron-containing media is system- and condition-specific.

draft_ledger.reference_answer:
Across the cited PFAS workflows, stock standards are generally prepared in-house from commercially obtained materials by dissolution in organic solvents at defined nominal concentrations. For example, Habib et al. report that analytical standards of perfluorocarboxylic acids were “purchased from Fisher Scientific … and standard stock solutions of 1000 µg/mL of PFCA were prepared in acetonitrile” (NQ03a_MMG001). Rahman et al. state that “all target PFCAs were obtained as solids, and stock solutions of individual PFCAs were prepared at a concentration of 1000 mg/L in methanol” (NQ03a_MMG005). Mel et al. describe that “individual PFAS stock solutions of 10 ppm were prepared in methanol” (NQ03a_MMG004), and Roque et al. prepared “concentrated stock solutions for all the PFAS … with a concentration of 600 mg L−1 for PFOA, 400 mg L−1 for PFBS, and 400 mg L−1 for PFOS” (NQ03a_MMG008). Pavithra and Chakraborty indicate that “the stock solution was initially made with methanol” (NQ03a_MMG006). In all of these cases, the methods sections provide the target nominal stock concentrations and solvents, but the nominal values themselves do not automatically constitute proof of concentration accuracy unless additional verification steps are described.

One of the cited studies explicitly demonstrates concentration accuracy of the prepared PFAS solutions. Pavithra and Chakraborty state that “the concentrations of the prepared PFOA solutions were verified using Gas Chromatography–Electron Capture Detector (GC–ECD) … after derivatization based on external calibration with derivatized PFOA standards, and the measured concentrations were within ±5% of the nominal values” (NQ03a_MMG006). This shows that the nominal concentrations of the prepared PFOA solutions were checked against an external calibration curve and found to agree within a defined tolerance. By contrast, several other workflows, such as Habib et al. (1000 µg/mL in acetonitrile; NQ03a_MMG001), Mel et al. (10 ppm in methanol; NQ03a_MMG004), and Rahman et al. (1000 mg/L in methanol; NQ03a_MMG005), provide nominal stock concentrations but, in the provided excerpts, do not describe independent analytical verification of those stock levels. These nominal labels therefore should not be interpreted as demonstrated accuracy or traceability in the absence of such checks.

Calibration and working standards are consistently prepared by controlled dilution of these stock solutions into specified matrices. Olomukoro et al. report that “working solutions were prepared by diluting the stock solutions with methanol and water (80:20, v:v) to achieve the desired concentrations” and that, for SPME calibration, “ultra-pure water was spiked at 5000 ng L−1 with the targeted analytes and diluted to give final concentration levels of 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, 20, 50, 250, 500 …” (NQ03a_MMG002), illustrating stepwise dilution from an initial spike concentration in ultra-pure water to a multi-point calibration series. Urtiaga et al. describe that “dilutions from the stock standard solutions were prepared in methanol/water (70:30 v/v) at seven concentration levels ranging from 1 ng/mL to 250 ng/mL and calibration curves were built in order to calculate the PFAS concentrations in real samples and to control the linear range of the instrumental response” (NQ03a_MMG007), again indicating preparation of a defined concentration series from stock solutions in a mixed solvent matrix.

Other studies use serial dilution of stock standards to construct calibration or working ranges. Shaikh et al. prepared PFOA calibration curves where “the standard calibration curves were obtained for higher PFOA (0.5 – 25 mg/L) and lower PFOA (5 – 500 µg/L) concentration ranges using standards prepared by high grade PFOA solutions,” with “concentrations … prepared by serial dilution of the standard stock solution of 50 mg/L and 1 mg/L for higher and lower concentration ranges respectively” (NQ03a_MMG003). Rahman et al. state that “working standards of PFCA mixtures or individual PFCAs were prepared by diluting stock solutions appropriately to either 10 or 1 mg/L and were also kept refrigerated at 4 °C” (NQ03a_MMG005), and Mel et al. note that “the working solutions for the sorption experiments were prepared by the dilution of the stock standards to achieve the desired concentration” (NQ03a_MMG004). Roque et al. indicate that “all the solutions used for the adsorption tests have been prepared by dilution of these stock solutions with ultrapure water” (NQ03a_MMG008), while Pavithra and Chakraborty describe that “Milli-Q water was used to formulate all subsequent working solutions” from a methanol stock (NQ03a_MMG006). Together, these examples show that calibration and experimental standards are generated from stock solutions by serial or stepwise volumetric dilution into methanol/water mixtures or high-purity water matrices, which is intended to preserve the proportionality and accuracy of concentrations across the calibration range.

Several of the workflows incorporate measures that support contamination control and preservation of standard concentrations. Use of high-purity aqueous matrices is common: Olomukoro et al. obtained “ultra-pure water … from a Milli-Q system” (NQ03a_MMG002) and used it both for spiking during calibration and in methanol/water working solutions; Pavithra and Chakraborty note that “Milli-Q water was used to formulate all subsequent working solutions” (NQ03a_MMG006); and Roque et al. report that all adsorption-test solutions were prepared by diluting stocks with “ultrapure water” (NQ03a_MMG008). These practices help minimize exogenous PFAS background that could bias the apparent concentrations of calibration or working standards. Urtiaga et al. further describe method-level quality control: dilutions from stock standards in methanol/water (70:30) were used to build calibration curves “in order to calculate the PFAS concentrations in real samples and to control the linear range of the instrumental response,” and they state that “quality control and validation of the method were made using internal standards and recovery rates, method blanks and calibration linearity” (NQ03a_MMG007). The use of method blanks and calibration linearity checks helps detect contamination or drift associated with standards and ensures that the calibration response remains reliable over the concentration range.

Handling and storage conditions are also described in some cases in ways that can help preserve accurate concentrations. Mel et al. state that “all solutions were stored at 4 °C in polypropylene (PP) bottles” (NQ03a_MMG004), and Rahman et al. indicate that PFCA stock and working standards were stored in methanol at 4 °C and that working standards were “also kept refrigerated at 4 °C” (NQ03a_MMG005). While these details pertain primarily to solution stability rather than formal verification of concentration, refrigerated storage in suitable containers is consistent with efforts to prevent concentration changes that might arise from degradation or adsorption. Overall, the provided methods show that preparation of PFAS stocks and calibration standards relies on well-defined solvent systems and dilution schemes, with at least one study explicitly verifying concentrations against external calibration and others using high-purity matrices, blanks, and calibration quality checks to support accurate and uncontaminated standard concentrations. At the same time, several methods report only nominal stock concentrations without explicit verification, so nominal labels in those cases should be interpreted as target preparation values rather than inherently validated concentrations.

reference_answer_claim_map.reference_answer_excerpt: Habib et al. report that analytical standards of perfluorocarboxylic acids were “purchased from Fisher Scientific … and standard stock solutions of 1000 µg/mL of PFCA were prepared in acetonitrile” (NQ03a_MMG001). Rahman et al. state that “all target PFCAs were obtained as solids, and stock solutions of individual PFCAs were prepared at a concentration of 1000 mg/L in methanol” (NQ03a_MMG005). Mel et al. describe that “individual PFAS stock solutions of 10 ppm were prepared in methanol” (NQ03a_MMG004), and Roque et al. prepared “concentrated stock solutions for all the PFAS … with a concentration of 600 mg L−1 for PFOA, 400 mg L−1 for PFBS, and 400 mg L−1 for PFOS” (NQ03a_MMG008). Pavithra and Chakraborty indicate that “the stock solution was initially made with methanol” (NQ03a_MMG006).

Pavithra and Chakraborty state that “the concentrations of the prepared PFOA solutions were verified using Gas Chromatography–Electron Capture Detector (GC–ECD) … after derivatization based on external calibration with derivatized PFOA standards, and the measured concentrations were within ±5% of the nominal values” (NQ03a_MMG006). This shows that the nominal concentrations of the prepared PFOA solutions were checked against an external calibration curve and found to agree within a defined tolerance. By contrast, several other workflows, such as Habib et al. (1000 µg/mL in acetonitrile; NQ03a_MMG001), Mel et al. (10 ppm in methanol; NQ03a_MMG004), and Rahman et al. (1000 mg/L in methanol; NQ03a_MMG005), provide nominal stock concentrations but, in the provided excerpts, do not describe independent analytical verification of those stock levels.

Olomukoro et al. report that “working solutions were prepared by diluting the stock solutions with methanol and water (80:20, v:v) to achieve the desired concentrations” and that, for SPME calibration, “ultra-pure water was spiked at 5000 ng L−1 with the targeted analytes and diluted to give final concentration levels of 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, 20, 50, 250, 500 …” (NQ03a_MMG002), illustrating stepwise dilution from an initial spike concentration in ultra-pure water to a multi-point calibration series. Urtiaga et al. describe that “dilutions from the stock standard solutions were prepared in methanol/water (70:30 v/v) at seven concentration levels ranging from 1 ng/mL to 250 ng/mL and calibration curves were built in order to calculate the PFAS concentrations in real samples and to control the linear range of the instrumental response” (NQ03a_MMG007). Shaikh et al. prepared PFOA calibration curves where “the standard calibration curves were obtained for higher PFOA (0.5 – 25 mg/L) and lower PFOA (5 – 500 µg/L) concentration ranges using standards prepared by high grade PFOA solutions,” with “concentrations … prepared by serial dilution of the standard stock solution of 50 mg/L and 1 mg/L for higher and lower concentration ranges respectively” (NQ03a_MMG003). Rahman et al. state that “working standards of PFCA mixtures or individual PFCAs were prepared by diluting stock solutions appropriately to either 10 or 1 mg/L” (NQ03a_MMG005), Mel et al. note that “the working solutions for the sorption experiments were prepared by the dilution of the stock standards to achieve the desired concentration” (NQ03a_MMG004), Roque et al. indicate that “all the solutions used for the adsorption tests have been prepared by dilution of these stock solutions with ultrapure water” (NQ03a_MMG008), and Pavithra and Chakraborty describe that “Milli-Q water was used to formulate all subsequent working solutions” from a methanol stock (NQ03a_MMG006).

Use of high-purity aqueous matrices is common: Olomukoro et al. obtained “ultra-pure water … from a Milli-Q system” (NQ03a_MMG002) and used it both for spiking during calibration and in methanol/water working solutions; Pavithra and Chakraborty note that “Milli-Q water was used to formulate all subsequent working solutions” (NQ03a_MMG006); and Roque et al. report that all adsorption-test solutions were prepared by diluting stocks with “ultrapure water” (NQ03a_MMG008). These practices help minimize exogenous PFAS background that could bias the apparent concentrations of calibration or working standards. Urtiaga et al. further describe method-level quality control: dilutions from stock standards in methanol/water (70:30) were used to build calibration curves “in order to calculate the PFAS concentrations in real samples and to control the linear range of the instrumental response,” and they state that “quality control and validation of the method were made using internal standards and recovery rates, method blanks and calibration linearity” (NQ03a_MMG007). Mel et al. state that “all solutions were stored at 4 °C in polypropylene (PP) bottles” (NQ03a_MMG004), and Rahman et al. indicate that PFCA stock and working standards were stored in methanol at 4 °C and that working standards were “also kept refrigerated at 4 °C” (NQ03a_MMG005).

draft_ledger.reference_answer:
Across the provided studies, several container materials and storage practices are reported for PFAS-containing water samples, and these choices are tied to the specific matrices and analytical needs rather than a single universal standard.

For sample-container materials used at the water-sample collection stage (T01):

• High-density polyethylene (HDPE)
  – Hui et al. sampled landfill leachate at key locations in several landfills and, immediately after collection, divided the samples "into pre-cleaned and dried 1 L/5 L high-density polyethylene (HDPE) containers — HDPE minimizes adsorption of PFASs and meets requirements for trace organic pollutant sampling containers" [NQ07a_MMG004]. Here, the matrix is landfill leachate containing PFASs and dissolved organic matter (DOM), and HDPE is explicitly chosen to limit PFAS adsorption and to satisfy trace-organic sampling requirements.
  – Chen et al. describe landfill gas and groundwater sampling: condensate traps along the gas pipeline were set up "using HDPE bottles" and "Groundwater was sampled from a monitoring well using a Waterra ® inertial hand pump connected to HDPE tubing" [NQ07a_MMG001]. These HDPE bottles and tubing are used in landfill condensate and groundwater contexts where PFASs are subsequently characterized.
  – In a column-treatment experiment on groundwater, Hayman et al. collected effluent samples to quantify PFAS breakthrough by attaching "clean HDPE sample bottles" directly to the end of each effluent tube; the bottles were "rinsed with a small amount of the sample water three times, then left in place to fill" [NQ07a_MMG002]. The same type of precleaned HDPE bottles was used to collect effluent water for ancillary water-quality measurements [NQ07a_MMG002]. These uses are in a controlled laboratory or pilot-testing context, with low-level PFASs in groundwater-like matrices.

• Glass
  – In a non-target evaluation of drinking water contaminants at a pilot-scale treatment plant, Tisler et al. report that "Glass containers (800 mL volume), heated to 550 ◦ C for 5 h and subsequently acid washed, were used for sampling" [NQ07a_MMG005]. The matrix is untreated and treated groundwater in a pilot plant. The glass containers are extensively pre-cleaned by high-temperature heating and acid washing, consistent with trace-level analysis of PFASs and other contaminants.

• Polypropylene
  – In a pilot study on hydroxyl-radical-based advanced oxidation processes, Venkatesan et al. followed the EPA Method 537.1 framework and state that "Influent and effluent samples were collected directly in a 250 mL polypropylene bottle" and that "Trizma buffer solids were added in each sample bottle (1.25 g in 250 mL of water) prior to collection" [NQ07a_MMG006]. The context here is influent and effluent water from oxidation processes, with PFASs and their precursors measured; polypropylene bottles are used in conjunction with a buffering agent prescribed by the method.

These examples show that container choice varies by study: HDPE is used for landfill leachate, condensate traps, groundwater, and column effluent (with an explicit rationale of minimizing PFAS adsorption in leachate), glass is used for pilot-scale groundwater treatment sampling after high-temperature and acid cleaning, and polypropylene is used for influent and effluent sampling in an advanced oxidation pilot following EPA 537.1. The evidence therefore supports a context-dependent selection of container materials rather than a single universally mandated container for PFAS water sampling.

For storage conditions of PFAS water samples prior to extraction (T02):

• Landfill leachate and related landfill samples
  – Chen et al. report that samples associated with their landfill study (including groundwater and landfill-related waters collected with HDPE materials) "were stored below 4 ◦ C until analysis" [NQ07a_MMG001], indicating cold storage for PFAS stability.
  – In Hui et al., landfill leachate samples collected into HDPE containers at several landfills were first "temporarily stored in a designated low-temperature area (4 – 8 ◦ C) at the landfill entrance" and then retrieved "via full cold chain to prevent fluctuations in sample properties" [NQ07a_MMG003]. After transport, "they were immediately sent to the Refrigerated Sample Library … stored at a constant 4 ◦ C in a light-proof environment, and pretreatment and analysis experiments were initiated within 72 h of sampling to inhibit microbial impacts on DOM morphology and PFAS concentrations" [NQ07a_MMG003]. Thus, for leachate rich in DOM and PFASs, the authors use HDPE containers plus refrigerated, light-protected storage and initiate analysis within 72 hours, explicitly linking these conditions to preserving DOM morphology and PFAS concentrations and minimizing microbial effects.

• Treatment-column effluent from groundwater (Hayman et al.)
  – Effluent samples collected in HDPE bottles were "tightly capped and placed into a labeled zip‐top bag, then into a second zip‐top bag, and stored in a refrigerator until shipment … in coolers with double-bagged wet ice" [NQ07a_MMG002]. Here, PFAS-bearing column effluent is stored refrigerated and protected by double bagging and chilled shipment, again emphasizing low-temperature storage of the HDPE-bottled samples before analysis at an external laboratory.

• Groundwater at a treatment pilot plant (Tisler et al.)
  – For the glass containers used in the pilot plant, "All samples were stored at 4 ◦ C and prepared the same day or the day after sampling" [NQ07a_MMG005]. This indicates refrigerated storage at 4 °C and very short holding times between sampling and analytical preparation in a mixed-target (including PFAS) context.

• Advanced oxidation influent and effluent (Venkatesan et al.)
  – For the polypropylene bottles used in this advanced oxidation pilot, Venkatesan et al. state: "The samples were sealed properly and kept at 4 °C until extraction" [NQ07a_MMG006], indicating that PFAS-influenced influent and effluent waters are refrigerated prior to solid-phase extraction for PFAS analysis.

Taken together, these studies illustrate that PFAS-containing water samples in HDPE, glass, or polypropylene containers are routinely stored refrigerated at about 4–8 °C. In landfill leachate, additional measures such as light-proof storage and analysis within 72 hours are explicitly linked to maintaining DOM morphology and PFAS concentrations and limiting microbial activity. In other matrices (groundwater, column effluent, advanced oxidation influent/effluent), the focus is on maintaining samples at 4 °C and minimizing holding time (same day, next day, or until extraction) to preserve analytes prior to PFAS extraction and analysis.

No information in the provided evidence explicitly describes container materials or storage conditions for post-extraction PFAS extracts (T03 and T04), so extract-storage protocols (such as solvent composition, extract vial material, or long-term freezer conditions) cannot be specified from these records.

Within these limits, the available studies consistently support that container and storage choices for PFAS water samples are context-dependent—varying with matrix (landfill leachate vs. groundwater vs. treatment effluent), analytical method, and concerns such as PFAS adsorption, DOM preservation, and microbial activity—and do not establish any single container material as universally safe or mandatory for all PFAS sampling scenarios.
